instructions: Each passage has underlined portions. Choose the best alternative (or NO CHANGE). Some questions ask about the passage as a whole.

passages.title: The Evolution of Photography
passages.text: Photography has transformed from a technical curiosity into one of the most [1] influential mediums of communication in the modern world. When the first photographic image was captured in 1826 by Joseph Niépce, it required an exposure time of eight hours. [2] Today's digital cameras can capture thousands of images per second, revealing the dramatic shift [3] in technological advancement. The earliest photographs were black and white, and photographers had to carefully plan [4] each shot due to the limitations of the medium. Color photography wasn't widely available until the 1930s, when Kodak introduced Kodachrome film, a revolutionary process that allowed amateur photographers to capture vibrant, lifelike images. [5] Before this innovation, only professional studios could produce color photographs. The transition from film to digital technology in the late 20th century [6] marked another pivotal moment in photographic history. Digital cameras eliminated the need for chemical processing, making photography more accessible and immediate. [7] Smartphones have made the camera ubiquitous, with billions of people now carrying a device that can capture professional-quality images. [8] The rise of social media platforms have[9] transformed how people share and consume photographs. Instagram, founded in 2010, became a cultural phenomenon, where millions of users upload photographs daily. [10] The democratization of photography has also raised important questions about authenticity, privacy, and the manipulation of images in the digital age. [11] Professional photographers now compete with amateurs in ways that were unimaginable just decades ago. Yet paradoxically, [12] the abundance of images in our society may have devalued individual photographs; we scroll through thousands without pausing to truly see them. [13] Nevertheless, photography remains a powerful tool for documenting truth, preserving memories, and expressing artistic vision. [14] In the future, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and virtual reality [15] will continue to reshape how we capture and experience visual reality.

passages.title: The Impact of Sleep on Learning
passages.text: Recent scientific research has demonstrated that sleep plays a crucial role in consolidating memories and enhancing learning [16] abilities. During sleep, the brain undergoes a complex process [17] that transfers information from short-term to long-term memory. Students who get adequate sleep before exams [18] perform significantly better than those who stay up all night cramming. This finding has important implications for educational institutions and parents. [19] The average teenager requires eight to ten hours of sleep per night, yet many [20] teenagers get far less due to school schedules and social activities. Sleep deprivation can lead to decreased attention, slower reaction times, [21] and impaired decision-making skills. [22] Many schools have begun adjusting start times to later in the morning, recognizing that adolescent circadian rhythms naturally shift toward a later sleep schedule. Studies show that schools implementing [23] these changes have seen improvements in attendance, grades, and overall student well-being. [24] The consequences of chronic sleep loss extends beyond academic performance; it affects physical health, mental health, and emotional regulation. [25] Sleep is not a luxury but a biological necessity, as vital [26] as food and water for human survival. During REM sleep, also known as the rapid eye movement stage, the brain consolidates [27] emotional memories and processes complex information. During non-REM sleep, the body repairs tissues and restores energy. [28] The architecture of sleep consists of multiple cycles, each lasting approximately 90 minutes. [29] Disruptions to normal sleep patterns can cause serious health problems, including obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and depression. [30] Public health campaigns should emphasize the importance of sleep hygiene, promoting regular bedtimes, limiting screen time before sleep, [31] and creating dark, quiet sleeping environments. Teenagers, in particular, benefit from consistent sleep schedules that allow [32] their developing brains to function optimally. [33] Understanding the science of sleep has revolutionized [34] our approach to education and health. As our society continues to prioritize productivity and achievement, we must not [35] neglect the fundamental importance of restorative sleep for cognitive function and overall well-being. [36]

passages.title: Sustainable Architecture and Green Building
passages.text: Sustainable architecture represents a paradigm shift in how we design and construct buildings to minimize environmental impact [37] while maximizing occupant well-being. Traditional construction methods consume vast quantities of energy, water, [38] and natural resources. [39] Modern sustainable buildings employ [40] renewable energy sources such as solar panels and wind turbines to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. They also incorporate water-harvesting systems, [41] green roofs, and permeable pavements that reduce runoff and promote groundwater recharge. [42] One exemplary project is the Bullitt Center in Seattle, a six-story office building [43] that produces more energy than it consumes through solar panels installed on its facade and roof. [44] The building also features rainwater collection systems [45] that provide all water needed for occupant use. Green certifications, such as LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design), [46] have become industry standards for evaluating sustainable buildings. [47] Buildings certified as LEED Platinum have achieved remarkable reductions in carbon emissions, water consumption, [48] and waste generation compared [49] to conventional structures. However, sustainability in architecture [50] extends beyond technical systems; it encompasses social responsibility, community integration, and long-term environmental stewardship. [51] Architects must consider the lifecycle of building materials, from extraction through manufacturing, transportation, [52] and eventual disposal or recycling. Sustainable design also prioritizes human health through improved indoor air quality, natural lighting, [53] and thermal comfort. Workers in green buildings report higher productivity and satisfaction, [54] demonstrating that environmental responsibility and economic benefits can align. [55] The construction industry, [56] which accounts for nearly 40 percent of global carbon emissions, must undergo a fundamental transformation toward sustainable practices. [57] Governments worldwide have begun implementing building codes that require or incentivize sustainable construction methods. [58] Investment in green architecture is not merely an environmental imperative [59] but an economic opportunity, as energy savings and improved worker productivity [60] can offset initial construction costs within 5-10 years. [61] The future of construction depends on architects and builders embracing sustainable principles [62] as the standard practice rather than an optional premium feature. [63] As climate change accelerates, the urgency of this [64] transition becomes increasingly apparent. [65]

passages.title: The History of Jazz Music
passages.text: Jazz emerged in New Orleans in the late 19th century as a unique fusion of African musical traditions, European harmonic structures, [66] and American cultural experiences. The genre developed from [67] the cultural melting pot of a port city where enslaved African Americans, Creoles, [68] Caribbean immigrants, and European musicians [69] contributed to a revolutionary sound. Early jazz musicians played in brass bands, dance halls, and saloons, [70] creating music that emphasized improvisation, syncopation, and rhythmic complexity. The influence of blues and ragtime [71] provided the harmonic and rhythmic foundations for jazz development. [72] Louis Armstrong, often considered the most influential jazz musician of all time, [73] revolutionized the genre through his virtuosic trumpet playing and innovative vocal techniques. [74] Armstrong's improvisational style became [75] the model for countless jazz musicians who followed. The Great Migration of African Americans from the South to northern cities [76] spread jazz northward, and Chicago and New York became major centers of jazz innovation. [77] In the 1920s, known as the Jazz Age, [78] the music gained enormous popularity among both Black and white audiences. [79] Jazz became the soundtrack to the Roaring Twenties, reflecting [80] the cultural dynamism and social changes of the era. [81] The genre continued to evolve throughout the 20th century, spawning [82] diverse subgenres including bebop, cool jazz, modal jazz, and fusion. [83] Each innovation pushed the boundaries of what were considered musically possible, [84] challenging musicians and audiences to embrace new forms of artistic expression. [85] Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, and Herbie Hancock [86] are among the legendary figures who shaped jazz's trajectory. [87] Jazz influenced popular music globally, affecting rock and roll, hip-hop, [88] and contemporary music production. [89] Despite its African American roots and creation, [90] jazz became America's most significant cultural export, recognized worldwide as a distinctly American art form. [91]

passages.title: The Psychology of Decision-Making
passages.text: The human brain makes thousands of decisions every day, ranging from mundane [92] choices about breakfast to life-altering decisions about career and relationships. Cognitive psychologists have discovered [93] that our decision-making processes are far more complex [94] and biased than traditional economic theories suggested. Traditional economics assumed that humans are rational actors [95] who make decisions based purely on logical analysis of available information. [96] However, research by psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky demonstrated [97] that humans are susceptible to numerous cognitive biases that systematically distort [98] our judgment. One prominent bias is confirmation bias, [99] where people seek information that confirms [100] their existing beliefs while dismissing contradictory evidence. Another powerful bias [101] is the availability heuristic, where people overestimate the likelihood of events [102] that easily come to mind. [103] Loss aversion is a psychological tendency [104] where people are more motivated to avoid losing something than [105] to gain something of equivalent value. [106] This bias helps explain why investors often hold onto losing stocks [107] too long in hopes of recovering their losses. [108] Decision fatigue occurs when the quality of decisions deteriorates [109] after making many choices, a phenomenon that affects everyone from busy professionals [110] to shoppers in supermarkets. [111] The framing effect demonstrates that people's choices [112] are influenced by how options are presented rather than by their [113] objective value. [114] Presenting a medical treatment as having a 90 percent [115] success rate produces different decisions than presenting [116] the same treatment as having a 10 percent failure rate, [117] even though these statements are mathematically equivalent. [118] Understanding these biases and heuristics [119] can help individuals make more rational decisions [120] and recognize when emotions or cognitive shortcuts [121] are leading them astray. [122] Creating decision-making environments with adequate [123] time, minimal distractions, and access to accurate information [124] can help mitigate the influence of biases. [125] In professional and organizational settings, [126] awareness of these psychological principles [127] can lead to better policies, improved outcomes, [128] and more ethical decision-making practices. [129] As we face increasingly complex choices [130] in our interconnected world, understanding the psychology of decision-making [131] has never been more important. [132]
